name: Atlantic Puffin
fact: Puffins can hold dozens of sand eels in their bill at once — the record is 62 — thanks to a specially hinged jaw and backward-pointing tongue spines.

name: Razorbill
fact: Razorbills are monogamous and often pair for life, returning to the same cliff ledge each breeding year to raise a single chick.

name: Common Guillemot
fact: Guillemot eggs are pyriform (pear-shaped); this causes them to spin in a tight circle if nudged, preventing them from rolling off narrow cliff ledges.

name: Black Guillemot
fact: Unlike most auks, Black Guillemots rarely venture far from shore and typically nest in pairs or small groups rather than massive colonies.

name: Little Auk
fact: The Little Auk is a starling-sized winter visitor to the UK; it breeds in the high Arctic in colonies numbering in the millions.

name: Northern Gannet
fact: Gannets plunge-dive at speeds of up to 100 km/h; they have no external nostrils and use subcutaneous air sacs to cushion the impact.

name: European Shag
fact: Shags often stand with wings spread to dry; unlike many birds, their feathers are not fully waterproof, which helps them dive deeper by reducing buoyancy.

name: Great Cormorant
fact: Great Cormorants have been used by fishermen in Asia for over 1,300 years; a snare around the neck prevents the bird from swallowing larger fish.

name: Manx Shearwater
fact: These birds are incredibly long-lived; one individual was recorded still breeding at age 55, having flown an estimated 8 million miles in its life.

name: Sooty Shearwater
fact: Sooty Shearwaters undertake a massive 65,000 km figure-of-eight migration across the Pacific and Atlantic oceans each year.

name: Balearic Shearwater
fact: The Balearic Shearwater is Europe's most endangered seabird; it is Critically Endangered and breeds only on the Balearic Islands.

name: European Storm Petrel
fact: The name 'Petrel' is a diminutive of Peter, referring to St. Peter, because the birds appear to walk on water as they forage.

name: Leach’s Storm Petrel
fact: Leach’s Storm Petrels have a deeply forked tail and a bounding, erratic flight pattern that resembles a large butterfly or a nighthawk.

name: Northern Fulmar
fact: Fulmars defend their nests by spitting a foul-smelling stomach oil at intruders, which can ruin the waterproofing of other birds' feathers.

name: Great Skua
fact: Often called the 'Bonxie', this aggressive bird is a kleptoparasite, meaning it steals food from other birds by harassing them mid-air.

name: Arctic Skua
fact: Arctic Skuas are known for their spectacular aerial chases, forcing terns and puffins to drop their catch so the skua can steal it.

name: Pomarine Skua
fact: Adults in breeding plumage have unique 'spoons' — central tail feathers that are twisted 90 degrees and rounded at the ends.

name: Black-legged Kittiwake
fact: The Kittiwake is the most oceanic of our gulls, spending the entire winter out at sea and only returning to land to breed on sheer cliffs.

name: European Herring Gull
fact: The red spot on the adult's bill is a 'releaser' for chicks; they peck at it to signal the parent to regurgitate food.

name: Great Black-backed Gull
fact: The world’s largest gull; it is a formidable predator that can hunt and kill adult birds as large as a Puffin or a Manx Shearwater.

name: Lesser Black-backed Gull
fact: While many migrate to Africa or Iberia, increasing numbers of Lesser Black-backed Gulls now spend the winter in the UK.

name: Common Gull
fact: Despite the name, it is less common than the Herring Gull or Black-headed Gull; its name actually refers to its habit of feeding on common land.

name: Black-headed Gull
fact: The 'black' hood is actually dark chocolate-brown and is lost during the winter, leaving only a small dark spot behind the eye.

name: Mediterranean Gull
fact: Mediterranean Gulls have pure white wingtips, lacking the black 'ink-dipped' tips seen on most other UK gull species.

name: Little Gull
fact: The world's smallest gull; it can be identified in flight by the striking jet-black underside of its wings.

name: Arctic Tern
fact: The Arctic Tern sees more daylight than any other creature, migrating from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year.

name: Common Tern
fact: Known as the 'Sea Swallow' due to its long tail streamers and graceful flight, it is a frequent visitor to inland reservoirs and gravel pits.

name: Sandwich Tern
fact: The Sandwich Tern is the largest of our common terns and is easily identified by its shaggy black crest and yellow-tipped black bill.

name: Roseate Tern
fact: One of the UK's rarest breeding birds, it has a very pale plumage that can show a delicate pink flush on the breast during breeding season.

name: Little Tern
fact: The UK's smallest tern; it nests in shallow scrapes on beaches, making its eggs highly vulnerable to high tides and human disturbance.

name: Red-throated Diver
fact: Red-throated Divers are the only divers capable of taking flight directly from land; others require a long running start across the water.

name: Great Northern Diver
fact: While they are winter visitors to the UK, they are known in North America as Loons, famous for their haunting, yodelling calls.

name: Purple Sandpiper
fact: Almost exclusively a bird of rocky shores, this sandpiper is often found dodging spray from crashing waves as it hunts for small molluscs.

name: Ruddy Turnstone
fact: True to its name, this bird uses its wedge-shaped bill to flip over stones, seaweed, and debris to find hidden crustaceans and insects.

name: Sanderling
fact: Sanderlings are famous for their 'clockwork toy' running style, chasing retreating waves down the beach and sprinting back before the next one hits.

name: Dunlin
fact: The most common small wader in the UK; in winter, they form massive, synchronized flocks that twist and turn over estuaries like smoke.

name: Eurasian Curlew
fact: Europe's largest wading bird, easily identified by its incredibly long, down-curved bill and haunting, bubbling 'cur-lee' call.

name: Eurasian Oystercatcher
fact: Despite the name, they rarely eat oysters; they use their hammer-like orange bills to bash open cockles and mussels or probe for worms.

name: Common Redshank
fact: Known as the 'sentinel of the marsh' because its loud, piping alarm call warns all other birds whenever a predator (or human) approaches.

name: Ringed Plover
fact: To protect their nests on open shingle, adults will feign a 'broken wing' to lure predators away from their camouflaged eggs.

name: Grey Plover
fact: In flight, this species is easily identified by its black 'armpits' (axillaries), which contrast sharply with its otherwise pale underwings.

name: Red Knot
fact: Knots are incredible long-distance migrants; some UK wintering birds fly all the way from the Canadian Arctic to reach our mudflats.

name: Bar-tailed Godwit
fact: A world-record flyer; one individual of this species was recorded flying non-stop for 11 days from Alaska to New Zealand.

name: Whimbrel
fact: Similar to a Curlew but smaller with a shorter bill; its distinctive call is a rapid, seven-note tittering whistle.

name: Common Eider
fact: The UK's heaviest and fastest-flying duck; its famous down feathers are so insulating they are still used in high-end bedding.

name: Brent Goose
fact: These small, dark geese travel from Siberia to the UK to spend the winter feeding almost exclusively on coastal eelgrass.

name: Rock Pipit
fact: Unlike most small songbirds, the Rock Pipit is a coastal specialist, nesting on cliffs and feeding on tiny kelp flies among the rotting seaweed.

name: Greenshank
fact: A tall, elegant wader with a slightly upturned bill. They often hunt small fish by running through shallow water and snapping them up.

name: Long-tailed Duck
fact: A deep-diving sea duck that can reach depths of up to 60 metres to find molluscs and crustaceans on the ocean floor.

name: Slavonian Grebe
fact: In winter, these 'horned' grebes move to the coast; they are known for eating their own feathers to help protect their digestive tract from fish bones.

name: Velvet Scoter
fact: A large black sea duck that can be distinguished from the similar Common Scoter by the white wing-bar visible when it flaps.

name: Common Shelduck
fact: Looking like a cross between a goose and a duck, Shelducks often nest in abandoned rabbit burrows near the coast.
